clips.title: 2NF: Functional Dependencies and Partial Key Dependencies
clips.hook: Define functional dependency and use it to detect and remove part-key dependencies.
clips.summary: A functional dependency X→Y means each X value maps to exactly one Y value. A table is in 2NF when every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key. Player_Rating depends only on Player, so it moves to its own Player table.
clips.videoTitle: Learn Database Normalization - 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, 4NF, 5NF

quiz.question: Table has key (Player, Item_Type) and attributes Item_Quantity and Player_Rating. Which dependency violates 2NF?
options: Player → Player_Rating
Player, Item_Type → Item_Quantity
Player, Item_Type → Player
Item_Quantity → Item_Quantity
quiz.explanation: Player_Rating depends on only part of the composite key, which is a partial dependency. The fix is to decompose into Player and Player_Inventory.

clips.title: 3NF: Transitive Dependencies and Decomposition
clips.hook: Why 2NF isn't enough: a non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute.
clips.summary: Player_Rating depends on Player_ID only through Player_Skill_Level, so the key → skill level → rating chain is a transitive dependency. It permits inconsistency, so 3NF forbids it. The fix is a separate skill-level-to-rating table.
clips.videoTitle: Learn Database Normalization - 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, 4NF, 5NF

quiz.question: In Player(Player_ID, Skill_Level, Rating) with Skill_Level → Rating, what violation exists and what is the fix?
options: Transitive dependency; move Rating into a Skill_Level→Rating table
No violation, since Player_ID is a single-attribute key
Multivalued dependency; add a key
Partial dependency; split on Player_ID
quiz.explanation: Rating depends on a non-key attribute, so the table violates 3NF. Decomposing into Player and Skill_Levels removes the redundancy.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Resolving Data Hazards by Stalling and NOP Bubbles
clips.hook: How the RF stage stalls, injects NOPs, and detects hazards by comparing register fields.
clips.summary: Stalling holds the instruction in RF (and IF) until the producer has written back, while RF feeds NOPs into ALU as bubbles. Hazard detection compares RA/RB of the RF instruction against RC of instructions in ALU, MEM, and WB, excluding R31 and unused fields. Stalling raises effective CPI.
clips.videoTitle: 15.2.3 Data Hazards

quiz.question: What happens to the ALU stage when the RF stage is stalled?
options: The pipeline flushes entirely
It re-executes the previous instruction
It is also stalled with the same instruction
It receives a NOP bubble inserted by RF
quiz.explanation: The RF stage can't pass its instruction on, so it inserts a NOP with no side effects, creating a bubble.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Bypassing (Forwarding) to Avoid Stalls
clips.hook: Route the ALU output straight to the RF stage and see how bypass mux priority works.
clips.summary: The needed value often already exists in the datapath, e.g. in the ALU output when the producer is in ALU and the consumer in RF. Muxes at register read ports select from ALU, MEM, WB stages, with the most recent matching instruction taking priority, then the register file.
clips.videoTitle: 15.2.3 Data Hazards

quiz.question: If RF's source register matches destinations in both ALU and MEM stages, which value is bypassed?
options: The register file value
Either; they're equal
The MEM stage value
The ALU stage value, as it's the most recent instruction
quiz.explanation: The youngest producer holds the correct latest value, so priority is ALU, then MEM, then WB, then register file.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Full Bypassing Cost and Load-to-Use Stalls
clips.hook: Why even a fully bypassed pipeline must still stall on load-use.
clips.summary: Bypassing adds mux delay lengthening the clock period and extra wiring, trading against stalling's CPI cost. Load data is only available at WB in this pipeline, so an instruction using a load result immediately must stall two cycles even with full bypassing.
clips.videoTitle: 15.2.3 Data Hazards

quiz.question: Why can't full bypassing eliminate stalls for a load immediately followed by a dependent instruction?
options: The register file is too slow
Load data isn't available in the datapath until the LD reaches WB
Bypass muxes cannot select memory
R31 conflicts
quiz.explanation: The loaded value appears late, so the consumer in RF must wait, inserting NOPs even with all bypass paths.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Deeper Pipelines and Compiler Scheduling
clips.hook: How deeper pipelines worsen hazards and how instruction reordering hides load-use stalls.
clips.summary: More pipeline stages increase in-flight instructions, raising hazard likelihood and CPI. A compiler can move independent instructions between a load and its use, removing stalls, though only when independent instructions exist.
clips.videoTitle: 15.2.3 Data Hazards

quiz.question: How can a compiler remove a load-to-use stall?
options: Use fewer registers
Move independent instructions between the LD and its consumer
Remove the bypass muxes
Insert more NOPs
quiz.explanation: Independent instructions fill the delay so the LD reaches WB as the consumer reaches RF.

clips.title: From Bayes' Rule to the MAP Objective
clips.hook: Why maximizing likelihood×prior is the same as maximizing the posterior, and why P(X) drops out.
clips.summary: MLE maximizes P(x|θ). Adding a prior P(θ) and using Bayes' rule gives the posterior P(θ|x) = P(x|θ)P(θ)/P(x). P(x) does not depend on θ, so the posterior is proportional to likelihood×prior and the argmax over θ is unchanged. This lets us skip computing the evidence.
clips.videoTitle: Bayesian Maximum Aposteriori Estimation (MAP): Extending Maximum Likelihood Estimation

quiz.question: Why can P(x) be ignored when computing the MAP estimate?
options: P(x) is only negligible for large datasets
P(x) is always equal to 1
P(x) is equal to the prior
P(x) does not depend on θ, so it doesn't change the argmax over θ
quiz.explanation: P(x) is a constant with respect to θ. It rescales the posterior but does not move its maximizer.

clips.title: MAP Caveats: Prior Quality and MLE as a Special Case
clips.hook: MAP needs a good prior, and MLE is the limit of an uninformative prior.
clips.summary: MAP only helps if the prior is good, and a bad prior hurts the estimate. MLE is the special case of MAP with a maximally uninformative prior, meaning infinite variance. In that case the prior is flat and the MAP objective reduces to the likelihood.
clips.videoTitle: Bayesian Maximum Aposteriori Estimation (MAP): Extending Maximum Likelihood Estimation

quiz.question: Under what prior does the MAP estimate reduce to the MLE?
options: A maximally uninformative (flat, infinite-variance) prior
Any prior, once enough data has been collected
A prior with zero variance centred at the true value
A very informative Gaussian prior
quiz.explanation: A flat prior is constant in θ, so maximizing likelihood×prior is the same as maximizing the likelihood.

clips.title: Why a destructor forces you to write a copy constructor
clips.hook: Shallow-copied pointers lead to use-after-free and double-delete once a destructor frees the resource.
clips.summary: A destructor that frees a heap allocation balances new/delete, but the defaulted copy constructor copies the pointer bits, so two objects own one allocation. The result is use-after-free and double delete, so a destructor implies a copy constructor that duplicates the resource.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: A class owns an int* from new[] and has a destructor that calls delete[], but uses the implicit copy constructor. What goes wrong when 'NaiveVector w = v;' goes out of scope?
options: Compile error because copy is implicitly deleted
Memory leak because the destructor is not called for w
Both objects hold the same pointer, so the allocation is freed twice and v may be used after free
w gets a deep copy automatically
quiz.explanation: The implicit copy constructor copies member-wise, so the pointer is duplicated, not the pointee. Both destructors delete the same block.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Copy-and-swap: safe against aliasing and self-assignment
clips.hook: Why checking &rhs != this is not enough for assignment operators.
clips.summary: A naive assignment that frees the old state first breaks on self-assignment. Worse, it breaks when rhs is owned by *this, such as a child vector in a tree, where a self-check does not help. Copy-and-swap builds a complete copy of rhs before modifying *this, so any aliasing or ownership relationship is harmless.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: Why does an 'if (&rhs != this)' guard not make a free-then-copy assignment operator safe in general?
options: rhs can be a different object that is owned by *this, so freeing the old state destroys rhs
delete[] cannot be called after a comparison
The guard prevents move assignment
Comparing addresses is undefined behavior
quiz.explanation: If rhs lives inside memory owned by *this, for example a child vector of a node, freeing the old state frees rhs even though the addresses differ. Copy-and-swap copies first.

clips.title: RAII and exception safety: cleanup via stack unwinding
clips.hook: Why cleanup belongs in destructors: stack unwinding skips ordinary code but runs destructors.
clips.summary: When an exception propagates, the runtime unwinds the stack and destroys local objects without running the rest of each function body. Manual delete at scope end is skipped and leaks, whereas a guard object whose destructor deletes the pointer always runs. The example guard is still unsafe because it is copyable, so double-delete is possible.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: Why does putting delete[] in a destructor of a local object fix a leak when a callee throws?
options: Stack unwinding destroys local objects, which runs their destructors even though the rest of the function body is skipped
Exceptions automatically call delete on raw pointers
The compiler inlines the destructor into the catch block only
throw triggers the garbage collector
quiz.explanation: Unwinding ends the lifetime of locals, which invokes destructors. A manual delete statement after the throw point is never reached.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Rule of Zero: delegate resource management to members
clips.hook: Business-logic classes should write no special members. Only small single-purpose RAII classes do.
clips.summary: Classes that solve a domain problem should hold std::vector, std::string, unique_ptr or shared_ptr members and default every special member. Only small single-purpose resource classes, such as a file handle, unique_ptr or unique_lock, hand-write the destructor and copy/move operations.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: Under the Rule of Zero, which class should hand-write a destructor?
options: A class with two int members
A small FileHandle class that wraps a raw descriptor
Any class that has a constructor
A Customer class with a std::string and a std::vector<Order>
quiz.explanation: Only classes that directly own a raw resource need custom cleanup. Others delegate to RAII members and default everything.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Move constructors and the Rule of Five
clips.hook: How rvalue overloads let a class steal a resource, and why the moved-from state matters.
clips.summary: The move constructor is an overload picked for rvalues, so it can take the heap pointer and size and leave the source null and zero instead of allocating and copying. The Rule of Five adds move operations to destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment. They are needed for performance, not correctness, and the source must be left destructible.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: What must a hand-written move constructor for a pointer-owning class do to the source object?
options: Null out its pointer and reset its size so its destructor does not free the stolen resource
Call delete on the source pointer immediately
Leave its pointer unchanged so it can still free memory
Copy the data and then free the original
quiz.explanation: After stealing, the source must be in a valid empty state, or both destructors would free the same allocation.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Move assignment via copy-and-swap with std::move
clips.hook: How one idiom serves both copy and move assignment, and why std::move is needed on a named rvalue reference.
clips.summary: Copy-and-swap can implement move assignment by initializing the local copy from std::move(rhs), which calls the move constructor, then swapping. std::move is needed because a named rvalue-reference parameter is an lvalue. Self-check shortcuts still fail for subobject aliasing.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: In a move assignment operator taking NaiveVector&& rhs, why write NaiveVector copy(std::move(rhs))?
options: std::move allocates new memory
The compiler forbids copying in assignment
rhs is an lvalue inside the function because it has a name, so without std::move it would be copied
rhs is const
quiz.explanation: A named rvalue reference is an lvalue expression. The cast to rvalue selects the move constructor.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Rule of Four and a Half: by-value assignment and swap
clips.hook: Take the parameter by value to merge copy and move assignment, and why you must write swap.
clips.summary: A single assignment operator taking its argument by value lets the caller choose copy or move, removing duplication. The class then needs destructor, copy constructor, move constructor and this one operator, plus a custom swap. Without it, std::swap uses move assignment, which calls swap again and recurses infinitely.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: Why must a class using copy-and-swap in its move assignment provide its own swap?
options: std::swap is deprecated
The default std::swap uses move construction and move assignment, so move assignment would call swap which calls move assignment recursively
The compiler cannot find std::swap
swap must be virtual
quiz.explanation: std::swap is implemented with moves, including move assignment. If that assignment uses swap, infinite recursion results.

clips.title: unique_ptr and shared_ptr as RAII special members
clips.hook: What destructor, copy and move mean for unique_ptr and shared_ptr.
clips.summary: unique_ptr manages ownership of an allocation, so copy is deleted, move transfers and nulls the source, and assignment must delete the old pointee. shared_ptr manages a reference-count increment: the destructor decrements and frees at zero, copy increments, and move transfers without changing the count.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: What does copying a shared_ptr do in RAII terms?
options: Does nothing
Increments the reference count, which the destructor later decrements
Transfers ownership and nulls the source
Allocates a new copy of the pointee
quiz.explanation: shared_ptr manages a count increment. Copying acquires another one, and each destructor releases one.

clips.title: RAII without moves: empty states and lock_guard
clips.hook: Moves need a disengaged state, but RAII works with copy-only or even destroy-only classes.
clips.summary: Move operations need an empty or disengaged state so the source does not release the resource, as with null pointers or a unique_lock that does not own its mutex. RAII does not require moves: Rule-of-Three classes work, and lock_guard has no copy or move at all, just a constructor that locks and a destructor that unlocks.
clips.videoTitle: Back to Basics: RAII and the Rule of Zero - Arthur O'Dwyer - CppCon 2019

quiz.question: Is std::lock_guard an RAII class even though it has no copy or move operations?
options: Yes, but only if it is moved once
Yes, it acquires in its constructor and releases in its destructor, and nothing more is required
No, RAII only applies to heap memory
No, RAII requires move semantics
quiz.explanation: RAII is about tying release to the end of an object's lifetime. Copy and move are optional extras.

clips.title: SIGKILL, SIGSTOP and the kill utility
clips.hook: Why kill -9 always works while plain kill (SIGTERM) may not.
clips.summary: SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (19) cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. The kill utility sends any signal, defaulting to SIGTERM (15), which can be handled, hence the need for -9 to force termination.
clips.videoTitle: Signals: Make Ctrl+C Do Anything You Want

quiz.question: Why might 'kill <pid>' fail to terminate a process while 'kill -9 <pid>' succeeds?
options: kill without option sends SIGSTOP
-9 gives the process more CPU time
kill without option sends SIGTERM, which can be caught or ignored
SIGKILL is delivered through a different channel to the parent
quiz.explanation: Default is SIGTERM (15), handleable; SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored.

clips.title: Stop signals, SIGCONT and process groups
clips.hook: Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP; SIGCONT resumes; negative PIDs signal whole process groups.
clips.summary: Stop-type signals freeze a process until SIGCONT; Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP to the terminal's process. Processes belong to process groups, and kill with a negative PID signals every process in that group.
clips.videoTitle: Signals: Make Ctrl+C Do Anything You Want

quiz.question: What does kill(-1234, SIGTERM) do?
options: Fails because PIDs are positive
Sends SIGCONT to group 1234
Sends SIGTERM to process 1234 only
Sends SIGTERM to all processes in process group 1234
quiz.explanation: A negative pid targets the process group whose ID is the absolute value.

clips.title: Hardware faults delivered as signals
clips.hook: Divide-by-zero, illegal instruction and bad memory access become SIGFPE, SIGILL, SIGSEGV.
clips.summary: CPU detects faults and raises exceptions; the kernel then sends a signal to the offending process, which terminates itself via the default action. SIGSEGV's default action also dumps core.
clips.videoTitle: Signals: Make Ctrl+C Do Anything You Want

quiz.question: How does the OS typically handle a process that accesses invalid memory?
options: Sends SIGSTOP
Ignores it
Sends SIGSEGV, whose default action terminates and dumps core
Kernel kills it directly without signals
quiz.explanation: The CPU traps and the kernel sends SIGSEGV to the process.

clips.title: Chen notation: entities, diamonds, min/max participation
clips.hook: How Chen notation encodes max cardinality (1/N/M) and total participation with double lines.
clips.summary: Entities are boxes and relationships are diamonds. Each end shows a maximum (1 or N/M) and the minimum is encoded by line style: a double line means total (universal) participation, a single line means partial. M and N are used on different sides to avoid implying equal numbers.
clips.videoTitle: Entity Relationship Diagrams

quiz.question: In Chen notation, what does a double line between an entity and a relationship diamond denote?
options: Total participation: every entity instance must take part in the relationship
A many-to-many relationship
A foreign key constraint
A weak entity
quiz.explanation: Double line = minimum cardinality of at least one (total participation); a single line means participation is optional.

clips.title: Weak entities and partial keys in ER diagrams
clips.hook: How an entity's identity can depend on a parent entity's key, as with Order and Order Line.
clips.summary: A weak entity has an identifier that is only unique in combination with the key of its owner entity, e.g. Order Line is identified by (Order Number, Line Sequence Number). Chen notation shows this with a double-bordered box and relationship, and omits the borrowed key attribute.
clips.videoTitle: Entity Relationship Diagrams

quiz.question: What identifies an Order Line, a weak entity of Order?
options: Line Sequence Number alone
A system-generated photo filename
Order Number alone
Order Number combined with Line Sequence Number
quiz.explanation: The partial key Line Sequence Number is only unique within an order, so the full key combines it with the owner's key.

clips.title: Mapping an ERD to relational tables
clips.hook: Entities become tables, 1-M becomes FKs, and M-M needs a junction table.
clips.summary: Each entity becomes a table with its attributes as columns and PK/FK constraints. One-to-many and one-to-one relationships become foreign keys, while many-to-many relationships are resolved by an associative entity (e.g. PET OWNERSHIP) whose table holds two FKs, decomposing the relationship into two one-to-many relationships.
clips.videoTitle: Entity Relationship Diagrams

quiz.question: How is a many-to-many relationship between Person and Pet represented relationally?
options: A foreign key from Pet to Person
A junction table with foreign keys to both Person and Pet
A repeated-group column in Person
A foreign key from Person to Pet
quiz.explanation: A single FK cannot hold many-to-many, so an associative table with two one-to-many relationships is introduced.
